message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel numeric work – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific, machine‑learning, and other compute‑heavy tasks. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each very powerful with deep pipelines, sophisticated branch prediction, large caches, and complex control logic. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores arranged in SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) groups; each core is lightweight and optimized for throughput rather than latency. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) or reduced instruction set (RISC) with many features (branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution). | Very simple instruction set focused on arithmetic and data movement; often uses fixed‑function units for specific operations. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory interface, support for virtual memory. | Smaller per‑core caches, relies heavily on shared memory and registers; memory access patterns must be coalesced for efficiency. |
| **Parallelism** | Limited parallelism – a few threads per core, heavy emphasis on single‑thread performance. | Massive data‑parallelism – thousands of threads can run simultaneously, all executing the same instruction stream. |
| **Latency vs Throughput** | Optimized for low latency – quick response to individual instructions. | Optimized for high throughput – many operations completed per cycle, but higher latency per operation. |
| **Typical workloads** | Control flow heavy tasks, branching, I/O, operating system services, general application code. | Data‑parallel tasks like matrix multiplication, convolution, image processing, physics simulation, AI inference/training. |
| **Power consumption** | Higher power per core, but fewer cores overall. | Lower power per core, but many cores can lead to significant total power draw when fully utilized. |

In short, CPUs excel at handling diverse, irregular tasks quickly, while GPUs shine when you have a huge amount of similar calculations that can be performed in parallel. That’s why modern systems often combine both: the CPU orchestrates the program, and the GPU accelerates the heavy numeric parts.
